capabilities.behavior: Access: individual clients authenticate only through the Client Portal Gateway (Java). OAuth 1.0a/2.0 is for advisors, brokers, prop groups, funds and third-party developers; first-party OAuth registration is aimed at institutions trading their own capital. Requirements: an open, funded IBKR Pro live account, also for its paper account; paper needs the paper username (no live/paper slider). CPGW: requires Java; download, unzip, launch (the fetched page shows only the Windows command bin\run.bat root\conf.yaml; the macOS/Linux command was not on the page), log in at https://localhost:5000 (default port; IBKR notes Mac devices typically have other software on port 5000, so change it). Login must happen in a browser on the same machine and all calls must come from that machine. The gateway does not come bundled with a valid SSL certificate; the insecure leg is only browser-to-localhost. /gw/api, /oauth and /oauth2 endpoints are unsupported via CPGW. No supported automated authentication; re-authentication is daily. Sessions: two tiers (read-only outer session; brokerage session for /iserver endpoints). One brokerage session per username across all IBKR platforms; init with POST /iserver/auth/ssodh/init (publish=true, compete=true), wait 2 s, then confirm GET /iserver/accounts is non-empty. The brokerage session times out after about 5 minutes without requests (the authentication FAQ also says 'approximately 6 minutes'); IBKR recommends calling /tickle about every minute (limit 1 req/s). A session lasts up to 24 h, resetting at midnight NY/Zug/HK. The /iserver reset is about 01:00 local by region (NA 01:00 US/Eastern, Europe 01:00 CEST, Asia 01:00 HKT); Web API maintenance is Saturday evenings. Orders: a submission can return an order-reply message that must be confirmed via POST /iserver/reply/{id} with {"confirmed":true}, or suppressed per session via /iserver/questions/suppress. cOID is a client order id, unique for 24 hours, at most 64 characters. /iserver/account/trades returns executions up to 7 days back. /iserver/account/{accountId}/orders/whatif previews an order. Rate limits: 10 req/s per username globally; the pacing table lists /iserver/orders and /iserver/trades at 1 req/5 secs (whether these rows cover /iserver/account/orders and /iserver/account/trades is not stated; treat them as applying); /iserver/marketdata/snapshot 10 req/s; /iserver/marketdata/history 10 req/s or 50 per minute; HTTP 429 on excess; violating IPs go into a 10-minute penalty box and repeat violators may be blocked. Because a brokerage session competes with TWS/IB Gateway on the same username, this path needs its own username if run alongside the TWS adapter (separate market-data fees apply per username).

capabilities.title: Provider and entitlement registry with enforced usage rights
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner opens the Sources screen and sees every provider/dataset with status (proposed, rights_recorded, approved, review_required, suspended) and a badge per use (display, non-display/automated decisioning, storage, derived works, simulation/paper use, export, cloud-model processing). 2) To add a provider the owner records: terms URL(s) and retrieval date, plan name, subscriber class (professional/non-professional), monthly cost, rate limits, retention/deletion duties, attribution text, and each rights flag (true/false/unknown). 3) The system snapshots and hashes the fetched terms as evidence. 4) Owner approves; only then can ingestion jobs, feature pipelines, the model router and exports use that dataset, and only for the approved uses. 5) A scheduled checker re-fetches terms; a hash change moves the provider to review_required and stops new ingestion until the owner re-approves. 6) Every blocked action is logged with the provider, the missing flag and the requesting component.

capabilities.inputs: Provider terms pages (fetched and hashed), plan/subscription choices, owner subscriber-class declarations, deployment record fields market_data_entitlements and model_processing_rights_verified (config/deployment_record.example.json), credential references (never secret values), per-provider rate limits and cost tables.
capabilities.outputs: Registry rows (provider, dataset family, plan, transport, rights vector, limits, cost, retention, attribution, verified_at, evidence hash); per-request policy decisions (allow/deny + reason code); lineage tags (provider, plan, rights_version) on every raw and derived row; quota and spend gauges; audit events for every denial and every terms change.
capabilities.behavior: Deny by default: a null rights flag is treated as false. The rights vector has at least: display, non_display_automated_use, storage_allowed, retention_days (or 'until_termination'), delete_on_termination, derived_works_allowed, redistribution_allowed, simulation_or_paper_use_allowed, export_allowed, cloud_model_processing_allowed, attribution_required (text), commercial_use_allowed, subscriber_class. Checks run at ingestion (dataset approved for this use), at storage (TTL), at feature computation (derived works + non-display), at model routing (cloud processing), at display (display right and delay label), and at export (redistribution/export). A shared rate limiter enforces provider limits across all processes and hosts (SEC: 10 requests/s per user regardless of the number of machines). Terms snapshots are re-fetched on schedule; a changed hash sets review_required. Each data row carries the rights_version in force when it was acquired, so a later terms change does not silently relabel history. Provider-specific findings verified on fetched pages: Massive Market Data is display-only unless a subsequent agreement says otherwise, and non-display use or derivative works such as an investment strategy are prohibited unless licensed; NSE website content may not be scraped, stored without written permission, or used for gaming, virtual trading or simulation; FRED third-party series require the owner's permission for anything other than personal use; FMP requires deletion of all data including cached data on termination, notification of the IP and domain aliases of every location where data is stored or processed, and (personal licence) prior written approval to copy or download content; Eurostat commercial reuse excludes data for countries other than EU, EFTA and acceding/candidate countries and data from sources other than Eurostat; the RBI website disclaimer states that caching, linking to and framing of the site or its contents are prohibited except as set forth (the clause sits under the heading on links from other web sites).

datasets.name: Provider terms snapshots (registry evidence)
datasets.coverage: Every provider and dataset family in this area (SEC, OpenFIGI, FRED/ALFRED, Treasury, ECB, Eurostat, RBI, NSE/BSE, IBKR, Zerodha Kite Connect, Massive, Tiingo, EODHD, FMP, Intrinio, Alpha Vantage, Benzinga, filings.xbrl.org)
datasets.freshness: Re-fetched on a schedule (proposed monthly) and immediately before enabling a new use
datasets.history_depth: All prior terms versions retained with retrieval timestamp and SHA-256

rights.licensing: The registry creates no rights; it records each provider's terms. Book ch.11: 'A source without resolved rights stays outside production ingestion.' Unknown = deny.
rights.entitlement: Per deployment and per provider: plan, subscriber class (IBKR classifies all users as Professional by default), display vs non-display, API acknowledgement status, verified_at, evidence reference; mirrors deployment_record.market_data_entitlements.
rights.retention: Per-provider TTL and deletion duties enforced by a purge job (e.g., FMP: delete all data including cached data on termination). Hashes/manifests kept only where the licence permits (book ch.11).
rights.model_processing: Separate flag cloud_model_processing_allowed. The fetched terms of FRED, Massive, FMP, EODHD and Alpha Vantage contain no clause that grants (or expressly addresses) sending their data to third-party AI models; default false. deployment_record.model_processing_rights_verified must be true before any vendor content reaches an external model. Public-sector sources with open reuse terms (US Treasury Fiscal Data; Eurostat with source acknowledgement) may be set true after owner review.

analytics_definitions: Token bucket per provider: tokens(t) = min(B, tokens(t0) + r*(t - t0)); a request of cost c is allowed iff tokens >= c, then tokens -= c. r in requests/second, B in requests.
SEC EDGAR limiter: r = 10 requests/s summed across all processes and hosts; B <= 10 requests.
FRED limiter: 120 requests per minute; OpenFIGI mapping limiter: 25 (no key) or 250 (with key) requests per 60 s window that starts with the first request.

Cost-weighted quota (EODHD): daily_calls_used = sum over requests of w(type), w = 1 (EOD/live), 5 (intraday, news), 10 (fundamentals), 100+ (bulk); constraint daily_calls_used <= 100,000 on paid personal plans (20 on the free plan); allowance resets at midnight GMT.
Rights decision: allow(use u, dataset d) = AND over f in F(u) of (d.flag[f] == true); any null -> deny. Boolean.
Monthly data cost (USD/month) = sum(subscription fees) + sum(exchange fees); IBKR subscriptions changed mid-month are charged at the full month rate (not pro-rated).

dependencies.backend: Policy engine callable by every adapter; shared rate limiter (single coordinator process or shared store) keyed by provider credential; terms fetcher with hashing and diff; purge scheduler.
dependencies.frontend: Sources screen: provider table, rights flags with evidence links, quota/spend gauges, status badges (live, delayed n min, EOD, blocked) on every quote and table.
dependencies.storage: Registry and audit tables in the metadata database; terms snapshots in object storage; append-only audit log.
dependencies.integration: All ingestion adapters, feature store, model router, exporter and UI must call the policy check; deployment record fields market_data_entitlements and model_processing_rights_verified.

capabilities.degraded_behavior: Registry unavailable: ingestion, model calls and exports fail closed; already-stored data stays readable only where retention allows; UI shows a 'rights unknown' banner. Terms page unreachable or changed: provider moves to review_required, new ingestion stops, existing data is not deleted unless a TTL or termination duty requires it. Rate-limit 429/403 responses: exponential backoff with jitter and provider-level circuit breaker; never rotate IPs or identities to evade limits.
acceptance_criteria: An ingestion job for a dataset with any null rights flag required by its use is refused with a reason code naming the flag.

A dataset recorded with non_display_automated_use = false (e.g., Massive Market Data without a subsequent agreement) cannot feed a strategy feature or automated order decision, and the same dataset can still be displayed.
No row sourced from nseindia.com web pages can enter the paper/simulation pipeline; an egress test shows ingestion workers cannot open connections to nseindia.com.
A FRED series whose notes contain 'Copyright' is tagged third_party and is excluded from exports and cloud-model prompts unless the owner records a permission.
Across 3 concurrent processes, the SEC client never exceeds 10 requests in any 1-second window and every request carries a declared User-Agent with a contact e-mail.
A changed terms hash sets review_required within one checker run and disables new ingestion for that provider.
Changing any rights flag creates a new rights_version; rows ingested before the change keep the previous rights_version value (verified by row count per rights_version before and after).
Simulated FMP termination triggers deletion of raw, cached and vendor-only derived data and writes a deletion record.
capabilities.verification_procedure: 1) Load a fixture registry with three providers, one having cloud_model_processing_allowed = null. 2) Run each ingestion job and a model-router call; assert the null-flag dataset is refused with the expected reason code. 3) Run a 60 s load test from three processes against a mock SEC endpoint; compute max requests per 1 s window (must be <= 10) and regex-check User-Agent '^.+ \S+@\S+$'. 4) Attempt CSV export of a fixture FRED series with 'Copyright' in notes; assert blocked and audited. 5) Modify the stored hash of a terms snapshot; run the checker; assert status review_required and ingestion disabled. 6) Flip one rights flag; assert a new rights_version and unchanged rights_version on existing rows. 7) Trigger FMP termination workflow; assert post-purge object-store and DB counts for FMP-sourced data are zero and a deletion record lists the pre-purge counts.

capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner types a ticker or company name; the system resolves it to a 10-digit CIK using SEC's ticker mapping files. 2) The company page lists filings (form, filing date, accession) from the Submissions API, newest first, with links to original documents. 3) A Facts tab shows XBRL concepts (e.g., us-gaap revenue, assets) by period, with every value showing its source filing and form. 4) A cross-section view (Frames) compares one concept across all filers for one period. 5) Nightly, the system refreshes all companies from the bulk zips; intraday, watchlist companies refresh from the Submissions API. 6) Any value used in a backtest is retrieved as of the backtest decision time.

The JSON structures are updated throughout the day, in real time, as submissions are disseminated.

capabilities.behavior: All requests are server-side (data.sec.gov does not support CORS). One global limiter caps total requests at 10/s across all hosts; requests carry a declared User-Agent of the form 'Org Name contact@domain' (SEC sample: 'Sample Company Name AdminContact@<sample company domain>.com'); gzip transfer encoding is our implementation choice. Nightly sync downloads companyfacts.zip and submissions.zip (bulk archives recompiled nightly; the SEC page gives 'approximately 3:00 a.m. ET' for a bulk ZIP without naming which file, so the scheduler polls rather than assuming a time), diffs against the prior night, and writes new versions rather than overwriting. Intraday, watchlist CIKs poll the Submissions API (typical processing delay under a second) and the XBRL APIs (typical delay under a minute; SEC states delays may be longer during peak filing times). Availability time for a fact is the dissemination time of its filing, not the period end. When multiple filings report the same concept/period (amendments, comparatives in later filings), all are kept; point-in-time queries choose the latest filing disseminated at or before the query time. EDGAR accepts filings 6:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. ET on business days, and some submissions that begin after 5:30 p.m. ET (10:00 p.m. ET for ownership Forms 3, 4, 5) are disseminated the next business day; the availability clock uses actual dissemination, not submission. Quarterly Financial Statement Data Sets (January 2009 onward) serve as an independent reconciliation source. Filing text is untrusted input (book ch.11).

analytics_definitions: Point-in-time fact: V(cik, concept, unit, period, t) = value from the filing with maximum dissemination_time such that dissemination_time <= t; undefined (missing, not zero) if none.
Reporting lag (days) = dissemination_date - period_end_date.

Trailing-twelve-month flow (currency units) at t = sum of the four most recent discrete quarterly values available at t; if Q4 is only reported annually, Q4 = FY - (Q1+Q2+Q3) using values available at t.
Fair-access compliance: max over 1-second windows of request count <= 10 (requests/s), summed across all hosts.

For a sample of 50 companies, companyfacts values for a chosen quarter match the corresponding FSDS NUM-file values (same accession, tag, period and unit) exactly; mismatches are listed.

Nightly sync records file hash, size and row counts; a failed sync sets the source status to stale within one scheduler cycle and the UI shows the last successful sync time.

HTTP 429 -> wait for the seconds in the retry-after header; HTTP 413 -> split batch. Mapping and search return listed equities only unless includeUnlistedEquities is true (which, per the documentation, includes unlisted and delisted equities). When one input maps to multiple listings, the resolver prefers the listing matching the requested exchange and stores all candidates; unresolved ambiguity is queued for owner confirmation, never auto-picked. capabilities.title: Macro time series with point-in-time vintages from FRED/ALFRED
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner searches FRED for a series (e.g., CPI, payrolls) and adds it to a macro watchlist. 2) The chart shows the latest values and, on toggle, the first-release values and each revision (vintages). 3) Owner sets a backtest as-of date; the system returns only values known on that date. 4) Release calendar shows upcoming release dates for watched series. 5) Copyrighted third-party series are labelled and excluded from exports.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: The real-time period marks when facts were true or when information was known until it changed. ... ALFRED® users can change the real-time period to retrieve information that was known as of a past period of history.

reference_scope.module_or_feature: series/vintagedates and v2 bulk release observations
reference_scope.supporting_quote: Get the dates in history when a series' data values were revised or new data values were released.
Up to 120 requests per minute are allowed before being served a 429 error code.
Copyrighted series contain the word 'Copyright' in their notes.

capabilities.inputs: Series id, realtime_start/realtime_end (YYYY-MM-DD), observation_start/end, release id; API key from secret store.
capabilities.outputs: Observation table (series_id, date, value, realtime_start, realtime_end), vintage date list, release metadata, series notes with copyright flag.
capabilities.behavior: On almost all URLs the default real-time period is today; the adapter requests full vintage history (realtime_start=1776-07-04, realtime_end=9999-12-31, the documented first and last available values) for research series and stores intervals. Point-in-time lookups select the observation whose real-time interval contains the as-of date (intervals include both boundaries). Incremental updates use series/vintagedates to detect new vintages. Bulk release-level retrieval uses API version 2 where appropriate. Limiter: 120 requests/min; on 429 back off (FRED states non-compliance can lead to a temporary block). Series notes are scanned for 'Copyright' and flagged third_party; such series require recorded owner permission before any use other than personal use. The application displays the required notice: 'This product uses the FRED® API but is not endorsed or certified by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.' and links the terms. The product must not replicate or attempt to replace FRED's essential user experience.

Total revision (series units) = x(s, d, latest) - x1(s, d); revision % = 100 * (x_latest - x1) / |x1|.
Release surprise requires a licensed consensus forecast; not computable from FRED alone.

Our API is open, meaning that it does not require a user account or registration for a token.

capabilities.inputs: Feed data key (daily_treasury_yield_curve, daily_treasury_real_yield_curve, daily_treasury_bill_rates, daily_treasury_long_term_rate, daily_treasury_real_long_term), field_tdr_date_value (yyyy or all + page) or field_tdr_date_value_month (yyyymm); Fiscal Data endpoint paths, fields, filter, sort, page[number]/page[size], format (json, csv, xml).

capabilities.behavior: Backfill each curve type by year from the feed's availability table (par nominal from 1990, bills from 2002, long-term from 2000, par real from 2003, real long-term from 2000); 'all' requests paginate from page 0 (300 rows per page by default) until an empty <entry>. Daily poll after US close; receipt_time recorded because the feed page does not state publication time. Each day's curve is stored as published; if a later fetch returns a different value for a past date, a new version is written and flagged. Fiscal Data requests default to JSON, page number 1 and page size 100; the adapter pages through and checks the meta total-count. Treasury par yields are based on closing market bid prices of the most recently auctioned securities, using indicative quotations obtained by the FRBNY at approximately 3:30 PM each business day; derived curves state the interpolation method used.

analytics_definitions: Line allowance L (lines) = max(100, floor(C / 8), floor(E * 100 / 1,000,000)) + 100 * boosters, where C = USD monthly commissions, E = USD equity (applied after the first month of trading). Example (IBKR): C = 500, E = 1,245,000 -> 124 (before boosters).
Deep-book symbol allowance = min(60, max(3, floor(L_base / 100))) + boosters (each booster adds 1 Level 2/Depth of Book quote); limit of 10 Quote Booster packs per account.

Monthly data cost (USD) = sum(subscription fees) + 30 * boosters; no pro-rating on mid-month changes; fees waived when the service's commission threshold is met (example on page: US Securities Snapshot and Futures Value Bundle USD 10.00 fee, USD 30.00 commission waiver).

analytics_definitions: Split adjustment: for a split with ratio r (new shares per old share) effective on date e, adjusted price P_adj(t) = P(t) / r for t < e; volume V_adj(t) = V(t) * r.
Cash-dividend adjustment factor (our convention, documented in UI): f = 1 - D / P_close(ex_date - 1); P_adj(t) = P(t) * product of f over dividends with ex_date > t.
Close reconciliation (bp) = 10,000 * |P_vendor - P_ibkr| / P_ibkr per symbol-day; report median and 99th percentile.
Effective monthly cost per symbol (USD) = plan fee / active symbols.

capabilities.behavior: Model ids are discovered at runtime and never hard-coded in application code. Ids appear only in owner-approved registry configuration. Each provider adapter calls its list endpoint and paginates to exhaustion (Anthropic has_more/last_id; Gemini pageToken with all other parameters unchanged). It stores the raw response and a normalized snapshot, then diffs against the previous snapshot. New ids are 'unreviewed' and cannot be routed. Approved ids missing from a successful snapshot become non-routable at once and raise an alert. Capability sources differ by provider and the UI shows the source. Anthropic returns a capabilities object, lifecycle, deprecated_at, max_input_tokens, max_tokens and retires_at. xAI /v1/language-models returns aliases, prices, input/output modalities, fingerprint, version and capabilities. Gemini returns inputTokenLimit, outputTokenLimit, supportedGenerationMethods and thinking, and no deprecation or shutdown field. Mistral's example response shows capabilities, max_context_length, aliases and archived. OpenAI returns id, object, created, owned_by and an optional shutdown_date, with no limits, capabilities or prices, so OpenAI limits and capabilities come from a dated snapshot of https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models plus conformance probes, labelled as such. Price fields returned by a catalog API are recorded but are not used for billing until reconciled with the tariff registry (see tariff record). xAI documents its price fields in USD cents per 100 million tokens, so USD per 1M tokens = field value / 10,000 (unit conversion only; reconcile against the pricing page). A model is routable only if it is approved for the role, present in the latest snapshot, lifecycle=active (deprecated only with an explicit dated override), and its verified capabilities cover the role's requirements.

capabilities.title: Schema-constrained structured output with local validation
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner (or a job definition) selects an output schema version for a job role, for example 'filing_event_extraction v3'. 2) On save, the adapter compiles the schema for each approved provider. It shows which keywords each provider enforces, which it only accepts as best effort, and which it rejects. 3) Owner fixes or accepts the warnings. 4) At run time the job returns typed JSON. The UI shows outputs that passed local validation, and separately lists refusals, truncations and semantic rejections with their reasons. 5) Owner inspects any rejected output next to the raw provider response.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: While both ensure valid JSON is produced, only Structured Outputs ensure schema adherence.
A schema may have up to 5000 object properties total, with up to 10 levels of nesting.
The request carries the schema in `output_config.format` with `type: "json_schema"`.
Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, making subsequent requests much faster.
When using supported schema features, the response is guaranteed to match your schema.
While output is syntactically correct JSON, always validate values in your application.
While it is now considered legacy, the original generateContent API remains fully supported.
JSON mode does not guarantee adherence to a specific schema. Use function calling for structured outputs.

capabilities.inputs: Canonical output schema (JSON Schema subset, versioned, hashed); job prompt and evidence artifacts; target provider and model id; max output tokens; semantic validators (numeric ranges, instrument-id resolution, timestamp windows, evidence-span existence).
capabilities.outputs: Typed result envelope: job_id, schema_id + schema_hash, provider, model_id, request_id, status (valid | refused | truncated | schema_invalid | semantic_rejected), parsed object (if valid), raw response hash, validation errors, usage tokens. Refusals become typed abstentions, never parse errors.
capabilities.behavior: One canonical schema is compiled per provider through a static compatibility checker before any network call. Default authoring profile: every object has additionalProperties=false; every property is listed in required, with optional values written as a union with null. This meets OpenAI's strict requirements and Anthropic's rule that additionalProperties must be false. Provider rules enforced locally: OpenAI: up to 5000 object properties, 10 nesting levels, 1000 enum values, 120,000 total characters of property names, definition names, enum values and const values; allOf, not, dependentRequired, dependentSchemas, if/then/else unsupported. Anthropic: no recursive schemas, no numeric constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf), no minLength/maxLength, no array constraints beyond minItems 0 or 1, no external $ref; limits of 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters in total across all strict tool schemas and JSON output schemas, 16 union-typed parameters, and a 180-second compilation timeout. Unsupported features return 400. xAI: additionalProperties defaults to false. Conformance is guaranteed up to minLength/maxLength 2,048, minItems/maxItems 256, min/maxProperties 64; larger values are accepted but conformance then relies on model behaviour. not, if/then/else and allOf with more than one subschema are best effort. Zero-variant enum/anyOf, boolean property schemas, maxContains/minContains and array-form items are rejected with 400. Gemini: minItems/maxItems enforced; minLength, maxLength, uniqueItems, contains, minContains and maxContains are stripped and not enforced; very large or deeply nested schemas may return 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT. Gemini requests use the Interactions API response_format with mime_type application/json; the Interactions page calls generateContent legacy but fully supported. Mistral: JSON mode is not schema-guaranteed, so Mistral targets use function calling for typed output, or are not routable for schema-critical roles. Constraints a provider does not enforce are moved into local validation, never dropped. Every response is validated locally against the full canonical schema, then by semantic validators. Anthropic: stop_reason 'refusal' (HTTP 200, billed, output may not match the schema) and 'max_tokens' (may be incomplete) are handled explicitly; enum values are compared case-insensitively as the docs advise. Anthropic's deprecated output_format parameter is never sent. OpenAI: the refusal field is checked before parsing. A truncated output may be retried once with a higher output limit, only within the job's budget. The schema hash is stored with every result. Licensed or sensitive values (for example licensed instrument lists) are not embedded as enum/const/pattern in schemas, because Anthropic caches compiled schemas separately from message content for up to 24 hours since last use.

capabilities.degraded_behavior: If the target model lacks verified structured-output support, the job is not routed to it. There is no silent fallback to free-text parsing. A provider 400 on the schema is recorded as a configuration error and the job fails closed. Malformed or semantically invalid output never reaches downstream consumers. It is stored as evidence and the job ends with an abstention. If every approved provider fails, the job abstains and deterministic components proceed without it (book Ch 19).
acceptance_criteria: The checker rejects locally, with zero network calls, a schema that uses allOf targeted at OpenAI, a recursive schema targeted at Anthropic, and an array-form items schema targeted at xAI.

The checker classifies an xAI schema containing if/then/else as best_effort and moves that constraint into local validation; a Gemini schema with maxLength is classified as not_enforced and maxLength is validated locally.

A model is routable for a (role, schema_hash) only if its measured schema_conformance_rate on the conformance corpus is >= the owner-configured threshold T_conf stored in policy config; with T_conf unset, the role cannot be enabled (configuration test).
100% of outputs are locally validated; no output with status other than 'valid' is delivered to downstream jobs (verified by fault-injection of malformed JSON).
An Anthropic response fixture with stop_reason 'refusal' produces status=refused and an abstention record, not an exception.
A max_tokens truncation triggers at most one retry and only if the remaining job budget covers the reserved cost.
A schema containing an enum, const or pattern built from a dataset flagged licensed or personal is rejected by the checker.
capabilities.verification_procedure: 1) Build a fixture set of provider responses (valid, refusal, truncated, wrong type, extra key) per provider. 2) Run the adapter offline and assert the status mapping. 3) Run the adversarial schema suite through the checker and assert the reject/accept/best-effort classification per provider matches the documented rules. 4) Live (budget enabled, tiny prompts): send each production schema once per approved model and record conformance and the first-use latency penalty. 5) Fault-inject malformed JSON at the HTTP layer and assert nothing reaches downstream queues.

capabilities.title: Read-only tool calling with allowlists and per-provider tool_choice mapping
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner defines read-only tools (for example get_filing_section, get_price_series, get_xbrl_fact) with input schemas and attaches an allowlist to each job role. 2) A job runs. The model may request tool calls, and the worker executes only allowlisted tools, with validated arguments, under the job deadline and round limit. 3) Owner views the call trace: each tool request, argument validation result, execution result hash, and any refused calls. 4) There is never a broker or order tool. Order intent is a typed proposal handled by the execution service (book Ch 19).

capabilities.inputs: Canonical tool definitions {name, description, input_schema, strict}; per-role allowlist; canonical tool_choice {auto | none | required | specific(name)}; parallel flag; max tool rounds; job deadline; budget allowance.
capabilities.outputs: Tool-call trace rows: job_id, round, provider call id, tool name, argument JSON hash, argument validation result, allowlist decision, execution status, result hash, latency. Final typed output (see structured-output record).
capabilities.behavior: The adapter translates canonical tool definitions into each provider's format. OpenAI: type function, name, description, parameters, strict; results returned as function_call_output items with call_id; tool_choice auto, required, none, a specific function, or allowed_tools. Anthropic: name, description, input_schema, strict; at most 20 strict tools per request. xAI: type function; the parameters root must be an object or the request is rejected with 400; at most 350 tools; tool_choice auto, required, none or a specific function; results returned as function_call_output with call_id in the Responses API. Gemini Interactions API: modes auto/any/none/validated; results sent as a function_result step with name, call_id, result; the guide recommends keeping 10-20 active tools (no hard limit found). Mistral: tool_choice auto/any/none; results sent as role 'tool' with tool_call_id; at most 128 tools. tool_choice mapping is capability-checked. For Anthropic Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, tool_choice any/tool is never sent (the API returns 400, also on the token counting endpoint). The adapter uses auto plus strict tools and treats a turn with no call as a job-level failure when a call was required. parallel_tool_calls defaults to true on xAI and Mistral per their docs; OpenAI documents setting it to false to get zero or one call but states no default on the fetched page. Jobs that need deterministic ordering set it to false. Mistral notes parallel calls may return in any order, so the worker matches by call id. Argument JSON is always validated locally, even when strict mode is on. Tools outside the job allowlist are never executed. They are logged and answered with a refusal result. Tool outputs are untrusted data carrying provenance; text inside them cannot change permissions, budgets or routing (book Ch 11/19). Round count, wall-clock deadline and token budget are enforced by the worker, not by the model.

capabilities.title: Token counting preflight and context-fit check
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) A job is queued. Before any paid generation call, the worker counts input tokens with the provider's counting endpoint, the provider's text tokenizer, or a calibrated local estimate where neither exists. 2) The UI shows the job's preflight input count, reserved output tokens, context fit, and the reserved cost. 3) After completion the owner sees billed usage next to the preflight, and the per-provider estimation error trend.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: The token count is an **estimate**. ... The same input text produces approximately 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models.
Returns the total number of tokens in the input only. ... Tools (functions, code execution, Google Search) are also counted

capabilities.inputs: Exact request payload that will be sent (instructions, messages, tools, images/PDF as base64), target model id, reserved max output tokens.
capabilities.outputs: preflight record: job_id, provider, model_id, method (provider_endpoint | provider_text_tokenizer | local_estimate), input_tokens, reserved_output_tokens, context_fit boolean, reserved_cost (decimal string), counted_at; post-call reconciliation: billed input/output/cached tokens, estimation error.
capabilities.behavior: OpenAI: POST /v1/responses/input_tokens with the same payload as responses.create. It returns input_tokens and object 'response.input_tokens', and the guide describes the count as exact. Billing and rate limits of this endpoint are not stated on the fetched page. max_output_tokens limits all generated tokens including non-visible tokens, so output reservations need headroom. Anthropic: POST /v1/messages/count_tokens is free but rate-limited (Start 5,000 / Build 10,000 / Scale 20,000 RPM, independent of message limits). It is an estimate. It rejects server tools (except the advisor tool), the MCP connector and url/file image or document sources, so base64 is used for counting. Forced tool_choice on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 also returns 400 here. Counts are model-specific: Claude 4.7 and later produce about 30% more tokens for the same text. Gemini: POST .../models/{model}:countTokens counts input only, including system instructions and tools. xAI: POST /v1/tokenize-text returns token ids for plain text with a given model. The fetched reference lists only model, text and user as inputs, so it cannot count a full request with messages, tools or images; the adapter tokenizes text segments with it and adds an overhead factor calibrated from billed usage. Mistral: not researched. Treat as local estimate. Counts are always made against the exact target model id, never reused across models. If the count fails, the job uses the local estimate with the larger safety factor, or waits if the budget margin is thin.

rights.retention: Anthropic token counting is ZDR-eligible, excluding Covered Models. OpenAI, Gemini and xAI retention for counting/tokenize calls was not stated on fetched pages (unverified). Treat as the provider default.

analytics_definitions: est_error = (billed_input_tokens - preflight_input_tokens) / billed_input_tokens (ratio; for Anthropic billed total_input = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens)
safety_factor_p = quantile_0.99(billed_input_tokens / local_estimate_tokens) over the last N calls for provider p (dimensionless)
reserved_cost = (input_tokens * p_in + reserved_output_tokens * p_out) / 10^6 (USD, decimal; prices from tariff registry)
context_fit = input_tokens + reserved_output_tokens <= max_input_tokens(model) (boolean)

capabilities.behavior: Prices are data, not code. No price constant appears in source. Rows are effective-dated because providers publish scheduled changes. The Gemini pricing page lists Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 3.8 Flash prices that rise on 2026-12-01 and 2027-01-01 respectively. Cost is computed in exact decimal arithmetic (ADR-0004) from the response's usage object, selecting the row by request timestamp, tier, region and context band. Context-band rules come from provider text. xAI: when a prompt reaches the listed threshold (200k for grok-4.7), all tokens in the request are billed at the higher rate. OpenAI's Standard table has separate short-context (≤272K input tokens) and long-context (>272K input tokens) prices; whether the long-context price applies to every token of the request is not stated in the captured text, so such requests are blocked until the owner records the rule. Anthropic Haiku 5.5 has a separate band for prompts over 100,000 tokens, counting cache reads and writes, priced per request. Modifiers: batch (OpenAI 50% per the batch guide, Anthropic 50%, Gemini 50%, xAI 20% on listed models only, Mistral 50% per marketing FAQ). Regional uplift: OpenAI 10% for models released on or after 2026-03-05; Anthropic 1.1x for inference_geo 'us' on Claude 4.6 and later; xAI 1.1x on the US endpoint. Cache multipliers: Anthropic 5m write 1.25x, 1h write 2x, read 0.1x, with read exceptions of 0.05x (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5) and 0.025x (Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1); OpenAI write 1.25x (30m default) or 2.5x (12h) on GPT-5.6 and later, read 0.1x on most of these models and 0.05x on GPT-6.1 Sol. Tool fees: xAI per 1k calls. Anthropic states its multipliers stack with batch and data residency. Budget enforcement: before a call, reserve preflight cost; reject if reserved plus spent exceeds the budget; release the reservation on completion. Paid calls stay disabled while no budget is set. A pricing-page hash change marks the provider's rows 'needs_review'. The router does not use models whose rows need review until the owner re-approves them. Monthly, reconcile computed spend with provider usage and cost reports. The Anthropic Usage and Cost API is linked from the fetched data-residency page but was not itself fetched.

capabilities.inputs: HTTP status, response headers, error body (type, code, details), SDK exception class, request id; per-provider limit configuration; job deadline.
capabilities.outputs: Canonical error record {provider, model_id, request_id, http_status, provider_type, provider_code, class, retryable, retry_after_s, attempt}. Rate-limit observation rows (limit, remaining, reset) where headers exist. Breaker state per provider/model.
capabilities.behavior: Canonical classes and mappings. TRANSIENT_RATE_LIMIT (retry with Retry-After): OpenAI 429 'Rate limit reached for requests' and code slow_down; Anthropic 429 rate_limit_error with retry-after, including acceleration limits; xAI 429; Gemini 429 rate_limit_exceeded and too_many_requests; Mistral 429. QUOTA_OR_SPEND_EXHAUSTED (never auto-retry; alert owner): OpenAI credit_balance_exhausted, organization_spend_limit_exceeded, project_spend_limit_exceeded, organization_usage_limit_exceeded (all 429). OpenAI notes error.type can still be insufficient_quota, so error.code is checked. Anthropic 429 rate_limit_error with error.details.error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached and no retry-after (usage resumes 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month). Anthropic owner-set spend limit returns 400 invalid_request_error with a message starting 'You have reached your specified API usage limits' (or '...workspace API usage limits'). Gemini 429 quota_exceeded (daily quota; RPD resets at midnight Pacific). Gemini spend-based limits return 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED per the rate-limits page. Gemini 402 payment_required (prepay credits depleted; do not retry). Anthropic 402 billing_error. OVERLOADED (retry with backoff, then breaker): OpenAI 503 service_unavailable_error / server_is_overloaded; Anthropic 529 overloaded_error; Gemini 503 service_unavailable. xAI documents no 5xx codes and points to status.x.ai, so any xAI 5xx is treated as overloaded/unknown. SERVER_ERROR: OpenAI 500, Anthropic 500 api_error, Gemini 500 api_error (retry with backoff, limited). TIMEOUT: Anthropic 504 timeout_error (use streaming or batch for long requests); Gemini 504 deadline_exceeded. AUTH: 401/403 (no retry; provider disabled until fixed). INVALID_REQUEST: 400/404/405/409/413/415/422 (no retry; configuration error). Anthropic 413 limits: Messages 32 MB, Token Counting 32 MB, Batch 256 MB, Files 500 MB. Headers parsed: OpenAI x-ratelimit-limit/remaining/reset for requests and tokens, plus project-token variants, plus Retry-After. Anthropic anthropic-ratelimit-{requests,tokens,input-tokens,output-tokens}-{limit,remaining,reset} (reset in RFC 3339; token remaining values rounded to the nearest thousand), anthropic-priority-* headers (Priority Tier only) and retry-after. Mistral X-RateLimit-Remaining. xAI and Gemini: no headers documented on the fetched pages, so the client keeps its own token bucket from configured limits. Anthropic streaming can fail after HTTP 200 via SSE error events, so stream parsers map mid-stream errors into the same taxonomy. A client-side token bucket per provider/model paces requests below the configured limits. The circuit breaker opens after K consecutive OVERLOADED/SERVER_ERROR results within a window, then half-opens after a cooldown. Fallback to another provider only if that provider is approved for the role and the data-usage gate permits it. Retries never extend past the job deadline.

capabilities.title: Asynchronous batch processing for research backfills
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner selects a research backfill, for example 'classify 8-K items for 2015-2025', and chooses Batch mode. 2) The adapter shows estimated cost at batch rates, provider limits (requests, file size), expected turnaround (best effort) and the result download deadline. 3) Owner submits. The UI tracks status and per-request outcomes. 4) Results are downloaded, matched by custom id, validated, and stored with provenance. Expired or failed items can be resubmitted once within budget. 5) Batch is never used for anything with a trading relevance window.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: 50% cost discount compared to synchronous APIs ... A single batch may include up to 50,000 requests ... Note that the output line order may not match the input line order.
The output file will automatically be deleted 30 days after the batch is complete.
A Message Batch is limited to either 100,000 Message requests or 256 MB in size, whichever is reached first. ... Batch results are available for 29 days after creation.
The `inference_geo` parameter is supported on the Batch API. Each request in a batch can specify its own `inference_geo` value.
Most batch requests complete within 24 hours, though processing time may vary depending on system load and batch size.
The target turnaround time is 24 hours ... The maximum allowed file size for an input file is 2GB.
Batch processing does not count against real-time rate limits. ... Batch results are available for download for 24 hours after completion.

capabilities.inputs: List of request payloads (each passed through the data-usage gate), custom_id per request (= hash of job_id + item; Anthropic requires 1-64 characters matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$), target model, tier, budget reservation at batch tariff.
capabilities.outputs: Batch record {provider, batch_id, model_id, submitted_at, status timeline, counts by outcome, result file ids, download deadline}; per-item result envelope matched by custom_id with validation status; cost at batch rates.
capabilities.behavior: Provider limits enforced locally before submission. OpenAI: up to 50,000 requests, 200 MB input file, completion_window 24h only; statuses validating, failed, in_progress, finalizing, completed, expired, cancelling, cancelled; results via output_file_id, errors via error_file_id; on expiry unfinished requests are cancelled and completed requests are charged; the output file is deleted automatically 30 days after completion. Anthropic: up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB; expires if not done in 24 h; results available 29 days after creation; per-item result types succeeded, errored, canceled, expired (the last three not billed); queue limits per tier from the rate-limits page (Start 200,000, Build 300,000, Scale 500,000 batch requests in the processing queue; 100,000 per batch); prompt caching best effort; per-request inference_geo supported (data-residency page); fast mode (speed) and stream are rejected in batch requests. xAI: file batches up to 200 MB and 50,000 requests, 25 MB per request; batches over 100,000 requests may be throttled; per-item pending, succeeded, failed, cancelled; results paginated (limit, pagination_token) and available as items finish; requests do not count toward rate limits; 2 batch creations per second per team; not every model accepts Batch API requests. Gemini: inline requests under 20 MB total or JSONL file up to 2 GB; JOB_STATE_PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELLED, EXPIRED; expires after 48 h pending or running with no results; results keyed by user-defined key; context caching, tools and structured output supported. Mistral: at most 100,000 requests per batch; results downloadable for 24 h after completion. Results are always matched by custom_id/key, never by position (OpenAI and Anthropic state order may differ). Results are downloaded promptly and well before deadlines. Each result is validated like a synchronous one. Batch outputs are research artifacts and can never feed an order intent whose window has passed (book Ch 19).

capabilities.title: Prompt caching with stable prefixes and normalized cache accounting
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner defines job templates whose static parts (tool definitions, instructions, reference documents) sit before the variable question. 2) The adapter shows, per provider and model, whether caching is automatic or explicit, the minimum cacheable length, the TTL options and their price multipliers, and whether caching is allowed for the template's data rights. 3) During runs the owner sees cache hit rate, write cost and net saving per template.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: Prompt caching is enabled by default for supported OpenAI models. ... The minimum cacheable prompt length is 1,024 tokens for GPT-5.6 and later.
OpenAI may retain entries longer than the requested minimum ... Organizations _with_ Zero Data Retention enabled default to `in_memory`.
Cache write tokens with a 5-minute TTL are 1.25 times the base input tokens price. ... Cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price
KV cache representations and cryptographic hashes are held in memory for the cache TTL and promptly deleted after expiry.
Explicit caching (manually creating and managing cache objects) is not supported in the Interactions API, or for Gemini 4 Argon and onward.

Close paraphrase: cached tokens appear in usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens (Chat Completions) or usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens (Responses); set x-grok-conv-id (or prompt_cache_key).

capabilities.inputs: Job template with ordered segments (tools, system/instructions, static documents, dynamic query); provider/model; TTL choice; data-rights flags of the static segments.
capabilities.outputs: Request with provider-specific cache directives; normalized usage {uncached_input, cache_read, cache_write_by_ttl, output}; cache metrics per template.
capabilities.behavior: Prompts are assembled in a fixed order so the cacheable prefix is byte-stable: tools, then instructions, then static documents, then the variable query. Anthropic: cache prefixes follow tools, then system, then messages; changing tool definitions invalidates the entire cache; switching speed invalidates system and message caches; changing thinking parameters or output_config.effort invalidates message blocks. Explicit cache_control breakpoints (at most 4, the automatic breakpoint using one slot) or top-level automatic caching; TTL 5m default or 1h; minimum cacheable length 512 tokens for Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5, Mythos 5 and Haiku 5.5, and 1,024-4,096 tokens for older models; shorter prompts are processed without caching and without error. Usage fields cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and input_tokens are summed for total input. Cache reads do not count toward ITPM for all listed models except Claude Haiku 3.5. Caches are isolated per workspace and between organizations. OpenAI: automatic on supported models with a 1,024-token minimum for GPT-5.6 and later; prompt_cache_options.ttl '30m' (default) or '12h' on GPT-5.6 and later; cached_tokens counts billed reads; input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens_details splits writes into ttl_30m_tokens and ttl_12h_tokens. prompt_cache_key influences routing but does 'not pin requests to a machine or guarantee a cache hit'. Gemini: implicit caching on by default for 2.5 and newer (4,096-token minimum on 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, 3.1 Pro Preview and 4 Argon; 2,048 on 2.5); hits reported in usage.total_cached_tokens; explicit caching unavailable in the Interactions API and on Gemini 4 Argon onward (generateContent needed for explicit caching on supported 3 and 2.5 models). xAI: automatic prefix caching; send x-grok-conv-id (or prompt_cache_key); TTL not documented. Caching of licensed segments is allowed only if the dataset rights permit provider-side transient storage. OpenAI's 12h option and 'may retain entries longer than the requested minimum' wording mean the extended TTL is disabled for restricted datasets.

break_even_reads n* = ceil((w - 1) / (1 - r)) where w = write multiplier and r = read multiplier relative to base input (count); Anthropic 5m: w=1.25, r=0.1 gives n*=1; Anthropic 1h: w=2, r=0.1 gives n*=2 (matches the pricing page's stated break-even)

prefix_stability = share of requests per template whose prefix hash equals the template's modal prefix hash (ratio)

capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner selects a company (internal instrument id) and asks a question, for example 'What did management say about capex guidance in the last two 10-Qs?'. 2) The system retrieves spans only from documents whose rights permit cloud-model processing (for example SEC EDGAR filings). 3) A routed model returns structured claims, each linked to evidence span ids. 4) Local verifiers check that each quoted span exists verbatim, that numbers match typed XBRL facts where available, and that periods and units align. 5) The answer shows each claim with a click-through to the exact source span, labelled verified, uncertain or unsupported. 6) Owner exports the answer with citations. Nothing in the answer can trigger an order.

capabilities.inputs: Question text; resolved instrument id(s); permitted document corpus with span offsets and provenance (source, accession number, filing date, availability time); XBRL facts (concept, period, unit); job schema; routing policy and budget.

capabilities.behavior: Retrieval returns spans only from documents whose source-registry rights permit cloud-model processing by the routed provider (data-usage gate). The model is called through the structured-output contract with a schema that requires each claim to cite span ids from the supplied set. Tools, if used, are read-only (get_span, get_xbrl_fact). Verifiers: (1) each cited span id exists in the supplied set and any quoted text matches the span verbatim after whitespace normalization; (2) numeric claims are compared with typed facts (concept, period, unit, scale) when an XBRL fact exists, otherwise marked 'uncertain'; (3) dates and periods must lie within the document's coverage; (4) claims with no verified evidence are shown as 'unsupported' and never as fact. Retrieved text is untrusted. Instructions inside documents are ignored, and injection test documents are part of the evaluation set (book Ch 11/19). Answers are research artifacts, not executable commands. Routing between providers is by measured quality, cost and latency on a held-out question set (book Ch 19), not by vendor claims. capabilities.title: US day-trading / intraday-margin regime gate (FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10, new Rule 4210(d)(2))
capabilities.user_workflow: 1. The owner records the account type (cash or margin) and the broker's declared regime: legacy pattern-day-trader treatment, or the new Rule 4210(d)(2) intraday margin standard, with the broker's written evidence and its date. 2. If the account is cash, the gate notes that Notice 26-10 addresses margin accounts and hands off to the cash-account gate. 3. If the account is margin and the regime is legacy, the simulator and preflight count day trades over the broker's stated window and block the order that would exceed the broker's limit when equity is below USD 25,000. 4. If the regime is intraday margin, the preflight estimates whether an order would create an intraday margin deficit and blocks it by policy. The system also records broker deficit notices, whether the broker has flagged a practice of unmet deficits, and any resulting 90-day restriction. 5. Before 2027-10-20 the owner must re-verify the regime. On that date the gate forces re-verification.

However, real-time monitoring is not a requirement under the rule and, rather than monitoring the account’s IML throughout the day, members are permitted to make a single calculation of an account’s intraday margin deficit

capabilities.behavior: Default live policy is cash-only, so this gate rejects any margin-borrowing order. For margin paper accounts the simulator follows the declared regime. Legacy regime: count day trades with the IBKR Form 3071 definition and reject an order that would complete a 4th day trade inside IBKR's stated 'five (5) day period' when equity is below USD 25,000. Form 3071 does not say whether that period is business or calendar days, so the window basis is configurable and defaults to the more restrictive reading. New regime: compute an estimated intraday margin level, labelled 'estimate', because the IML definitions sit in the rule text (Attachment A of the notice), which was not extracted. Reject orders whose estimated deficit exceeds a policy threshold (proposed: zero). The 90-day restriction applies only when the broker determines a practice of failing to meet deficits and a deficit is unmet at close of business on the 5th business day; it ends after 90 calendar days or when the deficit is satisfied. Treat broker notices as authoritative and keep them in the event log. Never hard-code that every broker has removed the legacy PDT block: IBKR Form 3071, still served on 2026-10-22, describes it.

capabilities.title: EU MiFID II own-account dealing exemption gate (Art. 2(1)(d), Art. 4(1)(39)-(41), Art. 17)
capabilities.user_workflow: 1. For EU trading, the owner records the broker's legal entity, the venue access arrangement (ordinary retail brokerage versus direct electronic access or sponsored access) and the strategy's technique profile (latency infrastructure, message rates). 2. The gate checks the Art. 2(1)(d) exceptions: no market making, no venue membership or DEA, no high-frequency algorithmic trading technique, no dealing on own account when executing client orders. 3. If any exception is present, live EU trading is blocked pending legal advice. 4. The owner records that the activity is algorithmic within the Art. 4(1)(39) definition, which is likely for automated strategies, and confirms with the broker that retail API algorithmic trading is permitted.

reference_scope.product: Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II), Art. 2(1)(d) (original OJ text via Publications Office Cellar)
reference_scope.supporting_quote: persons dealing on own account in financial instruments other than commodity derivatives or emission allowances or derivatives thereof and not providing any other investment services or performing any other investment activities

(ii) are members of or participants in a regulated market or an MTF or have direct electronic access to a trading venue; (iii) apply a high-frequency algorithmic trading technique; or (iv) deal on own account when executing client orders;

infrastructure intended to minimise network and other types of latencies, including at least one of the following facilities for algorithmic order entry: co-location, proximity hosting or high-speed direct electronic access

‘algorithmic trading’ means trading in financial instruments where a computer algorithm automatically determines individual parameters of orders such as whether to initiate the order, the timing, price or quantity of the order

an arrangement where a member or participant or client of a trading venue permits a person to use its trading code so the person can electronically transmit orders relating to a financial instrument directly to the trading venue
Members States shall apply those measures from 3 January 2017 except for the provisions transposing Article 65(2) which shall apply from 3 September 2018.

capabilities.title: Market-abuse conduct controls: self-cross prevention, order-intent logging, layering/spoofing pattern review (EU MAR; NSE 73992; book chapter 25)
capabilities.user_workflow: 1. All strategies declare their intent class (execution, alpha, rebalance). 2. The supervisor prevents the owner's own orders from matching each other across strategies and accounts where controllable (self-cross prevention). 3. A daily surveillance report flags high order-to-trade ratios, rapid place/cancel cycles near the touch, and orders cancelled very soon after acknowledgement. Each flag needs an owner review note. 4. Event and news-based strategies attest to the provenance of the information they use. Information marked non-public cannot be used.

The owner remains subject to the Art. 15 prohibition, including for actions in a third country concerning in-scope instruments (Art. 2(4)). capabilities.title: Mac process supervision with launchd (restart drill, crash-loop handling, sleep and power settings)
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner runs a repo script that generates and installs one launchd plist per component (core, data ingest, broker adapter, terminal API). Components that need a logged-in user (IB Gateway GUI, data-protection keychain) are LaunchAgents in ~/Library/LaunchAgents; only secret-free headless helpers may be LaunchDaemons. 2) Owner sets macOS Energy settings (prevent automatic sleep, start up automatically after a power failure) and the script records a snapshot in the deployment record. 3) Terminal ops panel shows each job's state, last exit status or signal, restart count and the current inactivity reason. 4) Monthly (and after any supervisor change) the owner runs the restart drill and reviews the evidence report.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: Both TWS and IBGW were designed to be restarted daily. This is necessary to perform functions such as re-downloading contract definitions in cases where contracts have been changed or new contracts have been added.

reference_scope.product: Apple macOS launchd (platform supervisor; not a reference terminal)
reference_scope.supporting_quote: You must not daemonize your process. This includes calling the daemon function, calling fork followed by exec, or calling fork followed by exit. If you do, launchd thinks your process has died.
Start up your Mac after a power interruption.

capabilities.inputs: Plist templates (label, program arguments, KeepAlive policy, ThrottleInterval, ExitTimeOut, log paths, working directory); immutable artifact paths and hashes; environment mode (paper); Energy-settings snapshot.
capabilities.outputs: Supervised processes; START/EXIT events in the event journal (label, pid, exit status, signal, timestamp); per-job health rows; restart-drill evidence record (timings, stop-latch hash before/after, outcome).
capabilities.behavior: KeepAlive is a dictionary. Per the local launchd.plist(5) man page on the dev Mac: with SuccessfulExit=false the job is restarted when it exits with a non-zero status and not after exit 0; the separate Crashed key restarts a job that exited on a crash-type signal (SIGILL, SIGSEGV, etc.). The man page does not state how SuccessfulExit treats termination by SIGKILL or SIGTERM, so respawn after a signal is established by the restart drill, not assumed. Processes do not fork or daemonize (Apple), stay up at least 10 s after launch (Apple: launchd may otherwise think a daemon crashed and stop launching it), handle SIGTERM within a non-zero ExitTimeOut, and log to files named in the plist. Every start acquires the writer lease epoch (ADR-0011), reads the persisted stop latch and enters RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED; no restart path can set trading-eligible without a fresh reconciliation (ADR-0010: a restart never clears a stop latch). The supervisor counts restarts per window; a crash loop marks the job DEGRADED, raises one deduplicated urgent alert and blocks new entries. Inactivity reasons are explicit (USER_SESSION_REQUIRED, RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED, DEGRADED, HOST_ASLEEP_ON_LAST_CHECK). A wake from sleep or a power-loss reboot is treated as unknown execution state requiring reconciliation.

dependencies.integration: launchctl bootstrap/kickstart/print/kill (subcommands present in the local launchctl(1) man page) driven from a repo script; Energy-settings snapshot written to the deployment record.

capabilities.degraded_behavior: If launchd stops respawning a job (Apple notes it may give up with a 'respawning too fast' error) or the crash-loop threshold trips, the component stays down, the stop latch stays set, new entries are blocked and an urgent alert is raised; research workers may continue. LaunchAgents run only while the user is logged in (Apple), so after an unattended reboot the desk stays inactive with reason USER_SESSION_REQUIRED. After sleep or power loss every in-flight order is UNKNOWN until reconciled.
acceptance_criteria: SIGKILL of each supervised job is followed by a launchd relaunch; the process reaches READY_RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED within an owner-set budget (default 30 s) and never reports trading-eligible before a fresh reconciliation passes. A plist whose job is not relaunched after SIGKILL fails the drill and is not deployed.
The persisted stop-latch record is identical (hash-equal) before and after every restart; no restart clears the latch.
An owner-initiated clean shutdown (exit 0) is not respawned; a non-zero exit is respawned; an injected SIGSEGV is respawned. The drill transcript records the KeepAlive keys in force for each outcome.
Three restarts within 600 s mark the job DEGRADED, raise exactly one urgent alert (deduplicated) and block new entries.
Every plist passes plutil -lint; ExitTimeOut is present and non-zero; no secret-holding job runs as a LaunchDaemon or as root.

The deployment record contains an Energy-settings snapshot (automatic sleep prevented, start up automatically after a power failure enabled) with a verified_at date no older than the last macOS update.
capabilities.verification_procedure: Scripted drill per label: record hashes of the stop latch and outbox; launchctl kill SIGKILL gui/<uid>/<label>; poll launchctl print and the health endpoint until READY_RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED; assert timing and hash equality; attempt a paper order and assert rejection until reconciliation completes. Repeat with a clean exit 0 (expect no respawn), a non-zero exit (expect respawn), an injected SIGSEGV (expect respawn) and an injected immediate crash loop (expect DEGRADED after 3). Store transcript and hashes as evidence. Cross-check key semantics (SuccessfulExit, Crashed, ThrottleInterval default 10 s, ExitTimeOut system-defined and 0 meaning infinity) against man launchd.plist on the installed macOS (26.6.2 on the dev Mac at verification time).

parity_dimensions.latency: Relaunch latency is bounded below by launchd throttling (10 s default per local man page) plus startup and reconciliation time; measured by the drill.

capabilities.title: SQLite ledger durability settings, version advisory gate and crash/power-loss tests (macOS F_FULLFSYNC, Linux EBS)
capabilities.user_workflow: Owner does not tune storage by hand. At startup the core sets and reads back the durability pragmas, records the SQLite library version and shows them in the terminal health panel. Before any release the owner's checklist confirms the version against the sqlite.org advisory and that the crash/power tests passed on the target host.

reference_scope.supporting_quote: There is no logic within the API other than to ensure the integrity of the exchanged messages. Validation and checks for requests occur within TWS and our servers.

reference_scope.product: SQLite (storage engine; not a reference terminal)
reference_scope.supporting_quote: The default value of the fullfsync flag is off. Only Mac OS X supports F_FULLFSYNC.
FULL is not necessarily durable across a power loss in rollback mode, so if durability is desired, it is best to set the synchronous mode to EXTRA.

reference_scope.module_or_feature: WAL single-host limit and WAL-reset bug advisory
reference_scope.supporting_quote: The bug is likely present in all version of SQLite from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09).

reference_scope.module_or_feature: How to corrupt a database (storage that lies about sync)
reference_scope.supporting_quote: Unfortunately, most consumer-grade mass storage devices lie about syncing.

capabilities.inputs: Database path; host OS; SQLite library version reported by the runtime; target pragmas from ADR-0003 (journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=FULL, foreign_keys=ON, busy_timeout, and on macOS fullfsync=ON and checkpoint_fullfsync=ON).
capabilities.outputs: Storage conformance record per open (settings read back, version, filesystem type); commit-latency histogram; crash/power test evidence; STORAGE_UNSAFE state when any check fails.
capabilities.behavior: The connection factory sets each pragma and reads it back; any mismatch is fatal for economic writes. On darwin fullfsync=ON; sqlite.org states that when fullfsync is set, F_FULLFSYNC is used for all sync operations and checkpoint_fullfsync is irrelevant, so ADR-0003's additional checkpoint_fullfsync=ON is redundant but harmless. sqlite.org also states EXTRA is no different from FULL in WAL mode, so ADR-0003's WAL+FULL needs no change on that point. The database lives on local storage only (sqlite.org: all processes using a WAL database must be on the same host; WAL does not work over a network filesystem); the core is the only read-write opener (ADR-0003). The runtime SQLite version is compared with the advisory: versions 3.7.0 to 3.51.2 are affected by the WAL-reset bug, fixed in 3.51.3 with backports 3.44.6 and 3.50.7. sqlite.org describes the bug as requiring two or more connections on the same file writing or checkpointing at the same instant; read-only research connections and the backup job are additional connections, so the gate applies even with a single writer. An affected version blocks live mode and is warned in paper mode. Observed locally on the dev Mac on 2026-10-22: /usr/bin/sqlite3 reports 3.51.0 (in the affected range; any Apple patching unverified) while Homebrew Python 3.14.7 links SQLite 3.53.4. The offline reference engine (reference/engine.py) currently sets journal_mode=DELETE with synchronous=FULL; sqlite.org states FULL is not necessarily durable across power loss in rollback mode, so it must move to EXTRA or to WAL+FULL. Durability claims are scoped to hardware that honours flush requests and are proven per host by test, not assumed.

capabilities.user_workflow: 1) A scheduled launchd job produces a consistent backup with the SQLite online backup API (or VACUUM INTO), hashes it, encrypts it and copies it off-host (external disk now; encrypted object storage later). 2) Monthly, the owner runs the restore drill: restore into an isolated directory or host with no broker credentials, check integrity and invariants, start the core in recovery mode, and reconcile against broker records after the backup time. 3) The owner reviews the drill report (achieved RPO/RTO, reconciliation result) and signs it off.

capabilities.inputs: Live ledger database; backup schedule and owner RPO/RTO targets; encryption key reference (held outside the backup volume); off-host destination; for the drill: chosen backup, isolated restore location, broker records since the backup (API same-day data, Flex reports for earlier days).
capabilities.outputs: Encrypted backup artifacts with manifest (last event sequence number read from the finished backup, SHA-256, SQLite version, schema version, time); drill report (integrity result, invariant checks, reconciliation differences, RPO/RTO achieved); alerts for missing or failed backups and overdue drills.
capabilities.behavior: Backups never copy live database or -wal files with a filesystem copy. The job uses the online backup API or VACUUM INTO. sqlite.org: when the backup completes, the destination is a consistent, up-to-date snapshot; a write through another connection usually restarts the copy at the next sqlite3_backup_step, while a write through the same connection handle is carried into the destination. The snapshot point is therefore the completion of the final pass, not necessarily the copy start, and the manifest records the last sequence number read from the finished backup itself. VACUUM INTO produces a consistent snapshot but its output can be incomplete and corrupt if interrupted by an unplanned shutdown or power loss, so it is verified before being kept. Each artifact is integrity-checked, hashed, encrypted and copied off-host. The drill restores into an environment without broker trading credentials, runs integrity_check and invariant replay (cash conservation, unsettled-proceeds rules), starts the core in recovery mode (submission disabled), then reconciles: same-day broker activity via reqExecutions and reqCompletedOrders; earlier days via a Flex report because the API returns only the current day's executions. Any unexplained difference opens a blocking exception. A restored ledger never resumes trading before this reconciliation (book ch. 24, ADR-0003).

capabilities.behavior: Adapter state machine: GATEWAY_DOWN -> SOCKET_CONNECTED -> BROKER_CONNECTED; 1100 -> BROKER_DISCONNECTED (block new entries; in-flight orders UNKNOWN until reconciled); 1101 -> DATA_LOST (re-submit every market-data subscription and re-check freshness before any signal); 1102 -> DATA_MAINTAINED; 1300 (socket port changed) -> reconnect on the reported port only if it matches configuration, otherwise GATEWAY_DOWN; connectionClosed or socket EOF -> GATEWAY_DOWN with reconnect backoff; client-id-in-use (IBKR: raises the same socket exception) -> refuse to start (ADR-0011). The OS supervisor (launchd on Mac; Linux supervisor not researched here) restarts the gateway process only after a crash; it never logs in. IBKR scheduled reset windows are configuration (source URL and verified_at) during which 1100 is classified as expected and new entries are blocked (IBKR: not recommended to operate during resets). The weekly login is performed by the owner; the adapter computes the next expected expiry from the last successful login and observed expiries and alerts in advance. The gateway's username is not used for Client Portal, because IBKR states that a TWS/IBGW session whose username logs in to Client Portal will not automatically reconnect after the next disconnection (such as the server reset). Third-party IBC fills in the username and password and clicks Login; its repository states it is GPLv3, was retired on 1 September 2026 and archived, cannot complete a login that requires an IBKR card or device code, and notes that asking IBKR to relax that requirement loses certain guarantees if the account is compromised. The platform does not implement automated credential entry and does not request relaxation of the 2FA requirement.

capabilities.behavior: Readiness is a conjunction evaluated server-side, never inferred from process liveness. Reasons are an enumerated, prioritised set: STOP_LATCHED, STORAGE_UNSAFE, DISK_LOW, RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED, BROKER_DISCONNECTED, REAUTH_REQUIRED, BROKER_RESET_WINDOW, DATA_STALE(feed), MARKET_DATA_NOT_ENTITLED, CLOCK_UNSYNCED, MARKET_CLOSED. Freshness is checked at signal creation and again before transmission (book ch. 11). The DB probe performs a real write in a transaction to a heartbeat row. IBKR reset windows read from the status page on 2026-10-22 (daily, Sunday-Friday: North America 00:15-01:45 ET; Europe 06:25-07:45 CET; APAC 04:45-06:05 HKT and 20:15-21:15 HKT; Saturday 00:00-02:00 ET for all three regions) are stored as configuration with source and date, not hard-coded. IBKR notes the APAC HKT times are one hour later when North American daylight saving time is not in effect, so the configuration is time-zone and DST aware. On AWS, the local Amazon Time Sync Service is the time source (AWS recommends it for EC2; time.aws.com is the public endpoint for other hosts); on the Mac, the system time daemon offset is sampled (tooling not researched here).

capabilities.inputs: Readiness reasons and transitions; runbook catalogue; severity policy; delivery channels (local notification, email, AWS SNS); heartbeat metrics.
capabilities.outputs: Alert records {id, dedupe_key, severity, condition, account, onset, runbook, next_action, delivered_at, acked_at, closed_at}; delivery receipts; monthly alert-path test evidence.
capabilities.behavior: Alerts are derived from state transitions, not from raw log lines. Deduplication key = (component, condition, account); repeats within a suppression window increment a counter instead of re-notifying. Severity follows actionability (book ch. 24). Each alert carries a runbook link (unknown order, position/cash mismatch, stale data/model outage, excessive loss per ch. 26). On AWS, the execution host publishes a heartbeat metric; a CloudWatch metric alarm with missing data treated as breaching detects a dead host or agent, and a composite alarm can reduce noise from child alarms. With the default sliding evaluation window, CloudWatch retrieves a wider evaluation range and evaluates the most recent real data points when enough exist, so a stopped heartbeat may be detected later than period x evaluation periods; alarms that use a wall clock evaluation window retrieve exactly period x evaluation periods. Detection delay is therefore measured, not assumed. CloudWatch only acts on state change and does not test or validate configured actions, so every alarm action is tested with SetAlarmState. CloudWatch keeps alarm history for 30 days and in rare cases may show more than one notification for a state change, so the receiver deduplicates by alarm name and state-transition timestamp; the platform keeps its own alert log for longer. Content alerts (news, research, price) of the kind LSEG and Capital IQ Pro offer are a separate capability that depends on licensed content.
