capabilities.title: Secrets management: Mac Keychain and AWS Secrets Manager, broker credentials never stored, paper/live separation, rotation
capabilities.user_workflow: 1) Owner stores application secrets (data-vendor and model API keys, Flex token, alert-channel tokens) through a repo command that writes to the Mac Keychain (paper) or AWS Secrets Manager (deployed), never to files or environment dumps. 2) The broker password and 2FA are entered only by the owner into the IBKR login window. 3) The terminal shows each secret's age and owner-set rotation due date; rotation follows a runbook. 4) On suspected compromise the owner runs the incident action: latch stop, revoke, reconcile, rotate, restart (book ch. 23).

reference_scope.supporting_quote: Two Factor Authentication (2FA) is required for all users at Interactive Brokers.

reference_scope.module_or_feature: Platform session credentials in configuration file (pattern not replicated)
reference_scope.supporting_quote: necessitates the 'Login Username' and 'Password' to be entered in the configuration file.
The Bloomberg B-Unit app is a secure and convenient way for Bloomberg Anywhere users to authenticate to the Bloomberg Terminal
Programs that run outside of a user context, like a launchd daemon, must target the file-based keychain.
With Secrets Manager, you can set up automatic rotation as often as every four hours.
Most command shells offer features that could compromise your secrets, such as logging and the ability to see the last entered command.

capabilities.inputs: Secret values supplied by the owner interactively; secret metadata (name, environment paper/live, consumer component, rotation policy); IAM/keychain access policies.
capabilities.outputs: Secrets available only to allowlisted processes; secret-age and rotation status; access audit (CloudTrail on AWS); redacted logs.
capabilities.behavior: Class A (broker login password and 2FA): never stored or typed by software; entered by the owner into the IBKR login window. Class B (application secrets): on the Mac, stored with the SecItem API; components that need the data-protection keychain run as LaunchAgents in the owner's session because the data-protection keychain is only available in a user login context (TN3137). TN3137 also states that data-protection keychain access groups come from code-signing entitlements authorised by a provisioning profile, which needs an app-like bundle, so command-line components must be packaged and signed accordingly or use the file-based keychain. On AWS, secrets are stored in Secrets Manager encrypted with a KMS key, read by the execution role for specific secret ARNs only, cached client-side, with resource policies guarded by BlockPublicPolicy, access restricted with aws:SourceVpce where workable, and calls monitored via CloudTrail. Paper and live secrets live in separate names, accounts/roles and databases; a production-mode flag is validated against the actual credential identity (book ch. 23). Secrets never appear in prompts, repository files, screenshots, shell history or telemetry; log redaction is tested. Rotation is automatic where the provider supports API-driven rotation, otherwise manual by runbook with reminders. capabilities.title: Instance recovery and single-writer fencing: automatic EC2 recovery, manual ownership transfer, competing-session detection
capabilities.user_workflow: If the execution host fails, the owner is alerted. Host-level recovery (EC2 automatic recovery) may bring the same instance back; the desk restarts in reconciliation-required mode. Moving execution to another host or back to the Mac is a manual, audited ownership transfer: stop latch, release certificate, stop the old instance, reconcile, then grant ownership to the new deployment.

reference_scope.module_or_feature: Competing session as a cause of 1100
reference_scope.supporting_quote: Your TWS/IB Gateway has been disconnected from IB servers. This can occur because of an internet connectivity issue, a nightly reset of the IB servers, or a competing session.
This exception will also occur if an API client attempts to connect with a client ID that is already in use.
If successful, the instance recovery process will appear to the instance as an unplanned reboot.
Automatic instance recovery can recover an instance that fails a system status check. However, automatic instance recovery does not operate if only the instance status check fails.

capabilities.inputs: Writer lease and execution-ownership records (ADR-0011); EC2 status-check metrics; release certificates; broker order tags; IBKR connectivity codes.
capabilities.outputs: Ownership state per broker account; recovery events; foreign-activity exceptions; transfer audit trail.
capabilities.behavior: Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default on supported instances; a recovered instance keeps its instance ID, public, private and Elastic IP addresses, instance metadata and attached EBS volumes, but data in RAM is lost and OS uptime resets to zero. After recovery the core starts in RECONCILIATION_REQUIRED with the latch preserved. An instance-status-check failure (not covered by automatic recovery) raises an alarm for the owner. There is no automatic multi-host failover (ADR-0011): a database lease cannot fence a host that still holds broker access, so infrastructure fencing (stopping the old instance) precedes any ownership grant. Every order carries the deployment:epoch tag; reconciliation treats untagged or foreign-tagged orders as foreign activity and latches the stop. A competing IBKR login with the same username is a documented cause of 1100 on the other session; the adapter treats an unexplained 1100 outside reset windows plus a foreign login indication as a possible second writer.
